entities.summary:
The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in 1928 by Hassan al-Banna in Ismailia, Egypt, represents a transformative force in the socio-political landscape of the Arab world and beyond. It arose in a period marked by the decline of the Ottoman Empire, colonial encroachments, and a growing desire for Islamic revivalism, positioning itself as a significant player in the movement towards political Islam. The organization has played a pivotal role in shaping modern Islamic thought and politics, influencing various Islamic movements globally and serving as a template for Islamist parties in regions from North Africa to the Middle East.

The Brotherhood's central achievements include its expansion from a small local movement to a transnational organization with branches in multiple countries. By the late 20th century, it had garnered millions of followers, establishing social welfare programs that provided education and health services, thus solidifying its grassroots support. Significant moments include its participation in the political processes of Egypt, particularly during the Arab Spring in 2011, which culminated in the election of Mohamed Morsi, the first democratically elected president of Egypt from the Brotherhood, before his ousting in 2013.

The legacy of the Muslim Brotherhood is profound, as it has influenced a generation of Islamist thought and political activity, creating a framework for modern Islamic governance and activism. Its rise and subsequent challenges have spurred debates around secularism, democracy, and governance in Muslim-majority societies, impacting the political landscape well into the 21st century. The organization has been both a source of reform and division, reflecting the complexities of balancing tradition and modernity in a rapidly changing world.
